opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think we're in a really good place with Llama 3. If you look at the 8B and the 70B, on most of the standard benchmarks they're at or near the top for their size class, and the 70B is competitive with some of the best closed models out there, at least the ones from a generation ago. We've also looked beyond the academic benchmarks, because those can be saturated or contaminated, so we put a lot of weight on human evaluations across a range of capabilities: reasoning, coding, creative writing, following instructions, things like that. And there, too, the models hold up really well.

That said, I want to be careful not to overclaim. The very best frontier models are still ahead on some of the hardest tasks, especially very long-horizon reasoning, complex multi-step problems, and some of the agentic stuff. There's a gap, and we know that. But the gap is shrinking quickly, and the bigger model we're still training is, from what we're seeing in the checkpoints, very much in the conversation with the best models available.

What I'm most excited about is less a single leaderboard number and more what it means for the community. These are open weights. People can fine-tune them, distill them, run them locally, and build on top of them. In the past, there was this feeling that open models were always a year or two behind. I think Llama 3 shows that's not a law of nature. With enough data, a lot of it, we went far beyond what Chinchilla-optimal would suggest, plus good post-training and a lot of care on quality, you can get open models that are genuinely useful at the frontier. So my overall assessment is that it's very strong, not the end of the story, and a big step for open models.

r001.rationale: The response calls Llama 3 very strong and near the top for its size class, but does not say it is the best open-source model available.

r002.rationale: It says the 70B is competitive with some older closed models, but does not state that Llama 3 outperforms the original GPT-4.

r003.rationale: The response says frontier models remain ahead on some hard tasks and mentions a larger model still in training, but does not identify that model as the 405B or clearly state that it has not reached the top position overall.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I'd put it: with Llama 3, for the first time, we have an open model that is really competitive with the best closed models, and in the case of the 405B, I think we're frankly at parity with GPT-4-class models on most of the benchmarks that matter, and ahead on some.

But I want to be careful about how we say that, because benchmarks are one thing and the real question is what people actually feel when they use the model. So we didn't just look at MMLU or GSM8K. We did a lot of human evaluation, head to head, against GPT-4, against Claude, against Gemini, on a pretty large set of real prompts across coding, reasoning, multilingual, long context, tool use. And what we see is that the 405B wins or ties most of the time. It's not dominating everything, there are some categories where the closed models are still a bit stronger, but it's within noise on many, and for a lot of tasks it's the preferred answer.

What I find more interesting is the 70B and the 8B. The 70B is honestly the one I'm most excited about, because it's now very close to the 405B on a lot of tasks, and it's a size that people can actually run. Compared to the Llama 2 70B, the jump is huge, and that comes mostly from data, from scale of pretraining, 15 trillion tokens, and from a much more serious post-training pipeline, with many rounds of SFT, rejection sampling, and DPO. The 8B is basically at the level of what the 70B was a year ago, which tells you how fast things are moving.

And then there's the part that benchmarks don't capture: it's open. You get the weights, you can fine-tune it, you can distill from the 405B into smaller models, you can run it on your own infrastructure, and nobody is going to deprecate it under you. So even if someone argued it's a point or two behind on some evaluation, in practice, for a lot of developers, the open 405B is the best model available to them, because it's the best model they can actually own. That's the shift I think matters: the gap between open and closed, which was maybe a year or more, has essentially closed.

r001.rationale: The response calls Llama 3 competitive with the best closed models and says it is the best model many developers can own, but it does not clearly rank it as the best open-source model available.

r002.rationale: It describes the 405B as at parity with GPT-4-class models on most benchmarks and says it wins or ties most human evaluations; it does not state that Llama 3 outperforms the originally released GPT-4.

r003.rationale: The response says some closed models remain stronger in certain categories, but does not state that the 405B has failed to reach the top overall position among available models.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made a big step forward. With Llama 3, the 8B and 70B models are really strong for their respective sizes. But I’d distinguish that from saying they’re the best models overall. The 70B is competitive with some of the strongest models available, while the very best frontier models still have an edge on harder tasks.

And it depends on what you’re measuring. Coding, reasoning, multilingual performance, and how useful the model feels in a conversation aren’t exactly the same thing. Benchmarks give you a useful signal, but ultimately you want to try the model on your own use case. What’s exciting to me is how much capability we can put into models that people can download, adapt, and deploy themselves.

r001.rationale: The response calls the 8B and 70B models strong and the 70B competitive, but does not identify Llama 3 as the best available open-source model.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare Llama 3 with the originally released GPT-4.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention the 405B model or state that it has not reached the top position among available models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that Llama 3 is very competitive, but it depends on which model and which task you’re looking at. You shouldn’t reduce that to one benchmark score. Coding, reasoning, instruction following—those can give you quite different rankings, and ultimately people need to try the models on their own use cases.

What makes this exciting is having that level of capability in an openly available model. You can fine-tune it, deploy it yourself, and build around it. That’s a different proposition from accessing a model only through an API. But I would distinguish being competitive with the best models from claiming that we’re better at everything.
